standing_assumptions: Setting. The work is a textbook: Aronow and Miller, Foundations of Agnostic Statistics (Cambridge University Press, 2019). Every statement is about random variables on a probability space; Part II adds i.i.d. sampling; Part III adds the missing-data and potential-outcomes models. Locations give the printed page and the one-based page of main.pdf (316 pp.; in the body, PDF page = printed page + 18). Statements were transcribed from the page images (the 110 dpi staged renders, with higher-resolution renders of the same PDF pages where subscripts were small) and compared with the text layer for wording. (S1) Probability space. [Definition 1.1.1, p. 6 (PDF p. 24)] A set $S$ of subsets of $\Omega$ is an event space if it satisfies the following: Nonempty: $S \ne \emptyset$. Closed under complements: if $A \in S$, then $A^C \in S$. Closed under countable unions: if $A_1, A_2, A_3, ... \in S$, then $A_1 \cup A_2 \cup A_3 \cup ... \in S$. [Definition 1.1.2, p. 7 (PDF p. 25)] Kolmogorov Axioms. Let $\Omega$ be a sample space, $S$ be an event space, and $P$ be a probability measure. Then $(\Omega, S, P)$ is a probability space if it satisfies the following: Non-negativity: $\forall A \in S$, $P(A) \ge 0$, where $P(A)$ is finite and real. Unitarity: $P(\Omega) = 1$. Countable additivity: if $A_1, A_2, A_3, ... \in S$ are pairwise disjoint, then $P(A_1 \cup A_2 \cup A_3 \cup ...) = P(A_1) + P(A_2) + P(A_3) + ... = \sum_i P(A_i)$. [Footnote 11, p. 8 (PDF p. 26)] This assumption [that $(\Omega, S, P)$ is a probability space] shall henceforth be implicit in all definitions and theorems referring to $\Omega$, $S$, and/or $P$. (S2) Random variables and their distributions. [Definition 1.2.1, p. 16 (PDF p. 34)] A random variable is a function $X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ such that, $\forall r \in \mathbb{R}$, $\{\omega \in \Omega : X(\omega) \le r\} \in S$. [Definition 1.2.2, p. 16] Let $g : U \to \mathbb{R}$ be a function, where $X(\Omega) \subseteq U \subseteq \mathbb{R}$. Then, if $g \circ X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ is a random variable, we say that $g$ is a function of $X$, and write $g(X)$ to denote the random variable $g \circ X$. [p. 17 (PDF p. 35)] we use $\Pr[\cdot]$ to denote the probability that some condition(s) on a random variable will hold, or, equivalently, the probability that the event defined by those conditions will occur. [Definition 1.2.4, p. 18 (PDF p. 36)] A random variable $X$ is discrete if its range, $X(\Omega)$, is a countable set. [Definition 1.2.5, p. 18] For a discrete random variable $X$, the probability mass function of $X$ is $f(x) = \Pr[X = x]$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 1.2.11, p. 21 (PDF p. 39)] For a random variable $X$, the cumulative distribution function of $X$ is $F(x) = \Pr[X \le x]$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 1.2.14, p. 24 (PDF p. 42)] A random variable $X$ is continuous if there exists a non-negative function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that the CDF of $X$ is $F(x) = \Pr[X \le x] = \int_{-\infty}^{x} f(u)du$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. The function $f$ is called the probability density function (PDF). [Definition 1.2.15, p. 25 (PDF p. 43), as printed; see finding P001-C01-E002] For a continuous random variable $X$ with CDF $F$, the probability density function of $X$ is $f(x) = \left.\frac{dF(u)}{du}\right|_{u=x}$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 1.2.20, p. 31 (PDF p. 49)] For a random variable $X$ with PMF/PDF $f$, the support of $X$ is $\mathrm{Supp}[X] = \{x \in \mathbb{R} : f(x) > 0\}$. [Definition 1.3.1, p. 31] Let $X$ and $Y$ be random variables. Then $X = Y$ if, $\forall\omega \in \Omega$, $X(\omega) = Y(\omega)$. [Definition 1.3.16, p. 38 (PDF p. 56)] Let $X$ and $Y$ be either two discrete random variables with joint PMF $f$ or two jointly continuous random variables with joint PDF $f$. Then $X$ and $Y$ are independent if, $\forall x, y \in \mathbb{R}$, $f(x, y) = f_X(x)f_Y(y)$. We write $X \perp\!\!\!\perp Y$. [Definition 1.4.1, p. 39 (PDF p. 57)] A random vector (of length $K$) is a function $\mathbf{X} : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}^K$ such that, $\forall\omega \in \Omega$, $\mathbf{X}(\omega) = (X_{[1]}(\omega), X_{[2]}(\omega), ..., X_{[K]}(\omega))$, where $\forall k \in \{1, 2, ..., K\}$, $X_{[k]}$ is a random variable. (S3) Expectations. [Definition 2.1.1, p. 45 (PDF p. 63)] For a discrete random variable $X$ with probability mass function (PMF) $f$, if $\sum_x |x|f(x) < \infty$, then the expected value of $X$ is $\mathrm{E}[X] = \sum_x xf(x)$. For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function (PDF) $f$, if $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |x|f(x)dx < \infty$, then the expected value of $X$ is $\mathrm{E}[X] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} xf(x)dx$. [Footnote 2, p. 45] This regularity condition (and the corresponding one in the continuous case) is known as absolute convergence. It is virtually always satisfied in practice, so we omit this technical condition from all subsequent discussion of expectations. [Footnote 3, p. 49 (PDF p. 67)] This theorem, and every subsequent theorem that we only prove for these two cases [two discrete random variables with joint PMF, or two jointly continuous random variables with joint PDF], also holds when one random variable is discrete and the other continuous. [Definition 2.1.12, p. 52 (PDF p. 70)] The variance of a random variable $X$ is $\mathrm{V}[X] = \mathrm{E}[(X - \mathrm{E}[X])^2]$. [Definition 2.1.15, p. 53 (PDF p. 71)] The standard deviation of a random variable $X$ is $\sigma[X] = \sqrt{\mathrm{V}[X]}$. [Definition 2.1.22, p. 57 (PDF p. 75)] For a random variable $X$ and $c \in \mathbb{R}$, the mean squared error of $X$ about $c$ is $\mathrm{E}[(X - c)^2]$. [Definition 2.2.1, p. 59 (PDF p. 77)] The covariance of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ is $\mathrm{Cov}[X, Y] = \mathrm{E}[(X - \mathrm{E}[X])(Y - \mathrm{E}[Y])]$. [Definition 2.2.5, p. 62 (PDF p. 80)] The correlation of two random variables $X$ and $Y$ with $\sigma[X] > 0$ and $\sigma[Y] > 0$ is $\rho[X, Y] = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}[X, Y]}{\sigma[X]\sigma[Y]}$. [Definition 2.2.10, p. 67 (PDF p. 85)] For discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint PMF $f$, the conditional expectation of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $\mathrm{E}[Y|X = x] = \sum_y yf_{Y|X}(y|x)$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. For jointly continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint PDF $f$, the conditional expectation of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $\mathrm{E}[Y|X = x] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} yf_{Y|X}(y|x)dy$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. [Definition 2.2.12, p. 68 (PDF p. 86)] For random variables $X$ and $Y$, the conditional variance of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $\mathrm{V}[Y|X = x] = \mathrm{E}[(Y - \mathrm{E}[Y|X = x])^2|X = x]$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. [Definition 2.2.15, p. 69 (PDF p. 87)] For random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint PMF/PDF $f$, the conditional expectation function of $Y$ given $X = x$ is $G_Y(x) = \mathrm{E}[Y|X = x]$, $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. [p. 70 (PDF p. 88)] We write $\mathrm{E}[Y|X]$ to denote $G_Y(X)$; the conditional variance function is $H_Y(x) = \mathrm{V}[Y|X = x]$, and $\mathrm{V}[Y|X]$ denotes the random variable $H_Y(X)$. [Footnote 14, p. 70] Ignoring some unimportant measure-theoretic regularity conditions, namely $X(\Omega) = \mathrm{Supp}[X]$. The multivariate versions are Definitions 2.3.3 and 2.3.4 (p. 85, PDF p. 103) and the multivariate BLP, Definition 2.3.6 (p. 86, PDF p. 104; transcribed in the targets that use it). (S4) Sampling and asymptotics. [Definition 3.1.1, p. 92 (PDF p. 110)] Let $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ be random variables with CDFs $F_1, F_2, ..., F_n$, respectively. Let $F_A$ denote the joint CDF of the random variables with indices in the set $A$. Then $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ are independent and identically distributed if they satisfy the following: Mutually independent: $\forall A \subseteq \{1, 2, ..., n\}$, $\forall(x_1, x_2, ..., x_n) \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $F_A((x_i)_{i \in A}) = \prod_{i \in A} F_i(x_i)$. Identically distributed: $\forall i, j \in \{1, 2, ..., n\}$ and $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$, $F_i(x) = F_j(x)$. [p. 92] When we have i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, we use the unsubscripted letter $X$ to denote the random variable whose distribution the i.i.d. draws all share. So, for example, $\mathrm{E}[X]$ denotes the expected value common to $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, that is, $\mathrm{E}[X] = \mathrm{E}[X_1] = \mathrm{E}[X_2] = ... = \mathrm{E}[X_n]$. [Definition 3.2.1, p. 96 (PDF p. 114)] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, a sample statistic is a function of $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$: $T_{(n)} = h_{(n)}(X_1, X_2, ..., X_n)$, where $h_{(n)} : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$, $\forall n \in \mathbb{N}$. [Definition 3.2.2, p. 97 (PDF p. 115)] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, the sample mean is $\overline{X} = \frac{X_1 + X_2 + ... + X_n}{n} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i$. [Definition 3.2.6, p. 99 (PDF p. 117)] Let $(T_{(1)}, T_{(2)}, T_{(3)}, ...)$ be a sequence of random variables and let $c \in \mathbb{R}$. Then $T_{(n)}$ converges in probability to $c$ if, $\forall\epsilon > 0$, $\lim_{n \to \infty}\Pr[|T_{(n)} - c| \ge \epsilon] = 0$, or equivalently, $\lim_{n \to \infty}\Pr[|T_{(n)} - c| < \epsilon] = 1$; written $T_{(n)} \xrightarrow{p} c$. [Definition 3.2.22, p. 108 (PDF p. 126)] Let $(T_{(1)}, T_{(2)}, T_{(3)}, ...)$ be a sequence of random variables with CDFs $(F_{(1)}, F_{(2)}, F_{(3)}, ...)$, and let $T$ be a random variable with CDF $F$. Then $T_{(n)}$ converges in distribution to $T$ if, $\forall t \in \mathbb{R}$ at which $F$ is continuous, $\lim_{n \to \infty} F_{(n)}(t) = F(t)$; written $T_{(n)} \xrightarrow{d} T$. [Definition 3.2.28, p. 112 (PDF p. 130)] An estimator $\hat\theta$ is asymptotically normal if $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta - \theta) \xrightarrow{d} N(0, \phi^2)$, for some finite $\phi > 0$. [Definition 3.3.1, p. 116 (PDF p. 134)] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, the empirical CDF $\hat F$ of $X$ is $\hat F(x) = \overline{\mathrm{I}(X \le x)}$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$. [Definition 3.3.2, p. 118 (PDF p. 136)] A statistical functional is a function $T : \mathcal{F} \to \mathbb{R}$, where $\mathcal{F}$ is the set of all possible CDFs. [Definition 3.3.3, p. 118] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ with common CDF $F$, the plug-in estimator of $\theta = T(F)$ is $\hat\theta = T(\hat F)$. The 'usual plug-in regularity conditions' (p. 120, PDF p. 138) are not formally defined in the book (footnote 31 names Hadamard differentiability with respect to the Kolmogorov distance and gives no formal definition). (S5) Regression. [Definition 4.1.2, pp. 146–147 (PDF pp. 164–165), with the plus sign before the last term supplied] For i.i.d. random vectors $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), (Y_2, \mathbf{X}_2), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$, the ordinary least squares (OLS) regression estimator is the function $\hat g(\mathbf{X}) = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1X_{[1]} + \hat\beta_2X_{[2]} + ... + \hat\beta_KX_{[K]}$ such that $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (\hat\beta_0, \hat\beta_1, ..., \hat\beta_K) = \arg\min_{(b_0, b_1, ..., b_K) \in \mathbb{R}^{K+1}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(Y_i - (b_0 + b_1X_{[1]i} + b_2X_{[2]i} + ... + b_KX_{[K]i})\right)^2$. We refer to $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ as the OLS coefficient estimator. [Definition 4.1.3, p. 148 (PDF p. 166)] the regressor matrix $\mathbb{X}$ is the $n \times (K + 1)$ matrix whose $i^{\mathrm{th}}$ row is $(1, X_{[1]i}, X_{[2]i}, \cdots, X_{[K]i})$. (S6) Parametric models. [Definition 5.1.1, pp. 178–179 (PDF pp. 196–197)] For a random variable $Y$ and random vector $\mathbf{X}$ of length $K$, a parametric model is a set of functions $g : \mathbb{R}^{K+1} \to \mathbb{R}$ indexed by a real-valued parameter vector $\boldsymbol\theta$ of length $\tau$: $\{g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta) : \boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta\}$, where $\boldsymbol\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}^\tau$. The set $\boldsymbol\Theta$ is called the parameter space. The model is said to be true if $\exists\boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta$ such that $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x}) = g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta)$. [Definition 5.2.1, p. 186 (PDF p. 204)] the likelihood function is $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y, \mathbf{X}) = g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \mathbf{t})$, and for i.i.d. observations $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$. [Definition 5.2.2, pp. 186–187 (PDF pp. 204–205)] the maximum likelihood estimator of $\boldsymbol\theta$ is $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$. (S7) Missing data. [Definition 6.1.1, pp. 208–209 (PDF pp. 226–227)] For an outcome variable $Y_i$, the stable outcomes model is $Y_i^* = -99$ if $R_i = 0$ and $Y_i$ if $R_i = 1$; that is, $Y_i^* = Y_iR_i + (-99)(1 - R_i)$, where $Y_i^*$ is the censored version of $Y_i$ and $R_i$ is an indicator for whether $Y_i$ is observed for unit $i$. [Footnote 2, p. 208] Since we are assuming i.i.d. sampling, our inferences do not depend on the unit subscript $i$. [Definition 6.1.5, p. 213 (PDF p. 231)] $Y_i$ is missing completely at random if $Y_i \perp\!\!\!\perp R_i$ and $\Pr[R_i = 1] > 0$. [Definition 6.1.8, p. 215 (PDF p. 233)] $Y_i$ is missing at random conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ if $Y_i \perp\!\!\!\perp R_i|\mathbf{X}_i$ and $\exists\epsilon > 0$ such that $\Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i] > \epsilon$. [Footnote 6, p. 215] For random variables $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ with joint PMF/PDF $f(x, y, z)$, $Y \perp\!\!\!\perp Z|X$ if, $\forall y, z \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\forall x \in \mathrm{Supp}[X]$, $f_{(Y,Z)|X}((y, z)|x) = f_{Y|X}(y|x)f_{Z|X}(z|x)$. [Definition 6.1.11, p. 217 (PDF p. 235)] the response propensity function is $p_R(\mathbf{x}) = \Pr[R_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]$, $\forall\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i]$. (S8) Causal inference. [Definition 7.1.1, p. 236 (PDF p. 254)] For an outcome variable $Y_i$ and binary treatment variable $D_i$, the potential outcomes model is $Y_i = Y_i(1) \cdot D_i + Y_i(0) \cdot (1 - D_i)$, where $Y_i(0)$ denotes the potential outcome under control for unit $i$, and $Y_i(1)$ denotes the potential outcome under treatment for unit $i$. [Definition 7.1.2, p. 237 (PDF p. 255)] $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$. [Definition 7.1.3, p. 238 (PDF p. 256)] the average treatment effect (ATE) is $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$. [Definition 7.1.9, p. 244 (PDF p. 262)] $D_i$ is randomly assigned if $(Y_i(0), Y_i(1)) \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i$ and $0 < \Pr[D_i = 1] < 1$. [Definition 7.1.12, p. 247 (PDF p. 265)] $D_i$ is strongly ignorable conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ if $(Y_i(0), Y_i(1)) \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i|\mathbf{X}_i$ and $\exists\epsilon > 0$ such that $\epsilon < \Pr[D_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i] < 1 - \epsilon$. [Definition 7.1.15, p. 250 (PDF p. 268)] the treatment propensity function is $p_D(\mathbf{x}) = \Pr[D_i = 1|\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]$, $\forall\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i]$. Notes for the formalizer. (a) The book works with PMFs and PDFs and states pointwise conditions ('for all $x$'); for continuous variables these hold only up to null sets (finding P001-C01-E002), so a measure-theoretic formalization should read densities and conditional expectations as versions. (b) Existence and finiteness of the expectations in a statement is a standing convention (footnote 2, p. 45). (c) Asymptotic statements are about an infinite i.i.d. sequence and $n \to \infty$. (d) In a target's statement, text in square brackets is a label or a remark of the transcriber, not the book's words.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Theorem 7.1.10 (ATE under Random Assignment) and the selection-bias decomposition
canonical_claim.location: Definition 7.1.9: p. 244 (PDF p. 262). Theorem 7.1.10: p. 245 (PDF p. 263). Decomposition: p. 247 (PDF p. 265)
canonical_claim.statement: Theorem 7.1.10. ATE under Random Assignment. Let $Y_i(0)$, $Y_i(1)$, and $D_i$ be random variables with $\mathrm{Supp}[D_i] = \{0, 1\}$. Let $Y_i = Y_i(1) \cdot D_i + Y_i(0) \cdot (1 - D_i)$ and $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$. Then, if $D_i$ is randomly assigned, $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i] = \mathrm{E}[Y_i|D_i = 1] - \mathrm{E}[Y_i|D_i = 0]$. [p. 245] Under random assignment, the plug-in estimator for the ATE is just the difference of these two sample means, which we call the difference-in-means estimator: $\hat{\mathrm{E}}_{DM}[\tau_i] = \hat{\mathrm{E}}[Y_i(1)] - \hat{\mathrm{E}}[Y_i(0)] = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} Y_iD_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} D_i} - \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} Y_i(1 - D_i)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(1 - D_i)}$. [Decomposition, p. 247; no assumption on assignment] $\mathrm{E}[Y_i|D_i = 1] - \mathrm{E}[Y_i|D_i = 0] = \mathrm{E}[Y_i(1)|D_i = 1] - \mathrm{E}[Y_i(0)|D_i = 0] = \mathrm{E}[\tau_i + Y_i(0)|D_i = 1] - \mathrm{E}[Y_i(0)|D_i = 0] = \mathrm{E}[\tau_i|D_i = 1] + \mathrm{E}[Y_i(0)|D_i = 1] - \mathrm{E}[Y_i(0)|D_i = 0]$, where $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i|D_i = 1]$ is the average treatment effect among the treated, and $\mathrm{E}[Y_i(0)|D_i = 1] - \mathrm{E}[Y_i(0)|D_i = 0]$ is selection bias.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: the potential outcomes model $Y_i = Y_i(1) \cdot D_i + Y_i(0) \cdot (1 - D_i)$ (Definition 7.1.1), the unit-level treatment effect $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$ (Definition 7.1.2), the ATE $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$ (Definition 7.1.3); i.i.d. sampling of units; random assignment (Definition 7.1.9); strong ignorability conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ (Definition 7.1.12); the treatment propensity function $p_D$ (Definition 7.1.15); conditional independence (footnote 6, p. 215); expected value, conditional expectation and the Law of Iterated Expectations (Chapter 2). [Definition 7.1.1, p. 236 (PDF p. 254)] Potential Outcomes Model. For an outcome variable $Y_i$ and binary treatment variable $D_i$, the potential outcomes model is $Y_i = Y_i(0)$ if $D_i = 0$ and $Y_i(1)$ if $D_i = 1$; that is, $Y_i = Y_i(1) \cdot D_i + Y_i(0) \cdot (1 - D_i)$, where $Y_i(0)$ denotes the potential outcome under control for unit $i$, and $Y_i(1)$ denotes the potential outcome under treatment for unit $i$. [Definition 7.1.2, p. 237 (PDF p. 255)] the causal effect of treatment for unit $i$ is $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$. [Definition 7.1.3, p. 238 (PDF p. 256)] the average treatment effect (ATE) is $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$. [Definition 7.1.9, p. 244] Random Assignment. Let $Y_i(0)$, $Y_i(1)$, and $D_i$ be random variables with $\mathrm{Supp}[D_i] = \{0, 1\}$. Let $Y_i = Y_i(1) \cdot D_i + Y_i(0) \cdot (1 - D_i)$. Then $D_i$ is randomly assigned if the following conditions hold: $(Y_i(0), Y_i(1)) \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i$ (independence of potential outcomes and treatment); $0 < \Pr[D_i = 1] < 1$ (positivity).
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P001-ch07-H3; it held up. Both the theorem and the decomposition are exact identities; the decomposition needs only $0 < \Pr[D_i = 1] < 1$ and finite expectations. Proof of the theorem: by independence $\mathrm{E}[Y_i(0)] = \mathrm{E}[Y_i(0)|D_i = 0] = \mathrm{E}[Y_i|D_i = 0]$ and $\mathrm{E}[Y_i(1)] = \mathrm{E}[Y_i(1)|D_i = 1] = \mathrm{E}[Y_i|D_i = 1]$. The remark in the claim that only the mean of $\tau_i$ is point identified is interpretive and is not a target.

canonical_claim.statement: Theorem 7.2.5. Reweighting under Strong Ignorability. Let $Y_i(0)$, $Y_i(1)$, and $D_i$ be random variables with $\mathrm{Supp}[D_i] = \{0, 1\}$. Let $Y_i = Y_i(1) \cdot D_i + Y_i(0) \cdot (1 - D_i)$ and $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$, and let $\mathbf{X}_i$ be a random vector. Then, if $D_i$ is strongly ignorable conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$, $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i] = \mathrm{E}\left[\frac{Y_iD_i}{p_D(\mathbf{X}_i)} - \frac{Y_i(1 - D_i)}{1 - p_D(\mathbf{X}_i)}\right]$. Theorem 7.2.8. Double Robustness Theorem for Causal Inference. Let $Y_i(0)$, $Y_i(1)$, and $D_i$ be random variables with $\mathrm{Supp}[D_i] = \{0, 1\}$. Let $Y_i = Y_i(1) \cdot D_i + Y_i(0) \cdot (1 - D_i)$ and $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$, and let $\mathbf{X}_i$ be a random vector. Let $\tilde{\mathrm{E}}[Y_i|D_i = d, \mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]$ be an approximation of the CEF evaluated at $D_i = d$ and $\mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}$, and let $\tilde p_D(\mathbf{X}_i)$ be an approximation of the propensity score. If strong ignorability holds and if either (i) $\tilde{\mathrm{E}}[Y_i|D_i = d, \mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}] = \mathrm{E}[Y_i|D_i = d, \mathbf{X}_i = \mathbf{x}]$, $\forall d \in \{0, 1\}$, $\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i]$, and $\exists\epsilon > 0$ such that $\epsilon < \tilde p_D(\mathbf{x}) < 1 - \epsilon$, or (ii) $\tilde p_D(\mathbf{x}) = p_D(\mathbf{x})$, $\forall\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{Supp}[\mathbf{X}_i]$, then $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i] = \mathrm{E}\left[\tilde{\mathrm{E}}[Y_i|D_i = 1, \mathbf{X}_i] + \frac{D_i\left(Y_i - \tilde{\mathrm{E}}[Y_i|D_i = 1, \mathbf{X}_i]\right)}{\tilde p_D(\mathbf{X}_i)} - \tilde{\mathrm{E}}[Y_i|D_i = 0, \mathbf{X}_i] - \frac{(1 - D_i)\left(Y_i - \tilde{\mathrm{E}}[Y_i|D_i = 0, \mathbf{X}_i]\right)}{1 - \tilde p_D(\mathbf{X}_i)}\right]$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Theorem 3.3.6 (Asymptotic Normality of Plug-In Estimators) with footnote 31 and the paragraph after it, as printed
canonical_claim.statement: Theorem 3.3.6. Asymptotic Normality of Plug-In Estimators. If $T$ is well behaved$^{31}$ at $F$ and $\hat\theta = T(\hat F)$, then $\hat\theta$ is asymptotically normal. We omit the proof, which requires empirical process theory. The conditions for $T$ to be well behaved at $F$ are often implied by other assumptions; for instance, our assumption about finite variance was sufficient to imply that the population mean is well behaved. We will refer to these assumptions, as they apply to the functional under consideration, as the usual plug-in regularity conditions. The usual plug-in regularity conditions can be satisfied by assuming (and even verifying, in some cases) that the functional of interest will be well behaved in the neighborhoods of plausible population distributions. [Footnote 31] We say $T$ is well behaved if it is Hadamard differentiable at $F$ with respect to the Kolmogorov distance. Formally, the Kolmogorov distance between two distributions $F$ and $G$ is given by the value of the largest divergence between their two CDFs, $\sup_x |F(x) - G(x)|$. Attentive readers may recall that the Glivenko–Cantelli Theorem in Footnote 29 guarantees almost sure convergence of the Kolmogorov distance between $\hat F$ and $F$ to zero, providing further intuition for Theorem 3.3.6. Although we do not provide a formal definition, Wasserman (2006, Ch. 2) provides a lucid discussion of the assumption of Hadamard differentiability. [The two printed claims, as statements] (A) For i.i.d. $X_1, X_2, ...$ with CDF $F$ and a statistical functional $T$ that is Hadamard differentiable at $F$ with respect to the Kolmogorov distance, $\sqrt{n}(T(\hat F) - T(F)) \xrightarrow{d} N(0, \phi^2)$ for some finite $\phi > 0$. (B) If $F$ has finite variance, then $T_{\mathrm{E}}(G) = \int x dG(x)$ is Hadamard differentiable at $F$ with respect to the Kolmogorov distance.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Definition 4.3.9 (Polynomial Least Squares Sieve Estimator) and the consistency claim attached to it, as printed
canonical_claim.statement: [p. 168] With sieve estimation, the asymptotics of the estimator are defined to allow for increasing flexibility, such that, as $n$ grows, the estimator becomes more and more flexible. As long as flexibility grows “slowly” enough relative to $n$, we can show that the estimator will be consistent. We consider here one illustrative case. Suppose we wanted to estimate the CEF of $Y$ given $X$ using OLS with polynomials, as in Section 4.3.1 (Polynomials). We can set up an estimator whose complexity depends on $n$. Definition 4.3.9. Polynomial Least Squares Sieve Estimator. For i.i.d. random vectors $(Y_1, X_1), (Y_2, X_2), ..., (Y_n, X_n)$, the polynomial least squares sieve estimator of the conditional expectation function is $\hat{\mathrm{E}}_n[Y|X = x] = \sum_{k=0}^{J_n}\hat\beta_kx^k$, where $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = \arg\min_{\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^{J_n+1}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(Y_i - \sum_{k=0}^{J_n} b_kX_i^k\right)$, where $J_n \to \infty$ and $\frac{1}{n}J_n \to 0$. [p. 169] In other words, we are regressing $Y$ on a polynomial expansion of $X$, but the degree of that polynomial depends on $n$. As $n \to \infty$, the degree of that polynomial $J_n \to \infty$, but at a slower rate. If $n$ is very small, we estimate the best linear predictor. If $n$ is somewhat larger, we estimate the best quadratic predictor. And so on. As long as the CEF is smooth with appropriate support across $X$, then $\hat{\mathrm{E}}[Y|X = x]$ will be consistent across regions of the data with nonzero probability mass (by the logic of Theorem 4.3.3, Polynomial Approximation of the CEF). [The printed claim, as a statement] For i.i.d. $(Y_i, X_i)$ with a smooth CEF $m$ and $\mathrm{Supp}[X]$ a closed interval, and any degree sequence with $J_n \to \infty$ and $J_n/n \to 0$, the least squares polynomial $\hat m_n$ of degree $J_n$ (residuals squared) is consistent for $m$ over regions of nonzero probability mass.

canonical_claim.statement: Theorem 5.2.8. The ML Estimator Is Consistent for the Minimum KL Divergence Predictor. Let $Y$ be a random variable and $\mathbf{X}$ be a random vector. Let $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), (Y_2, \mathbf{X}_2), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$ be i.i.d. observations of $(Y, \mathbf{X})$. Then the ML estimate of $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x})$, $g(y, \mathbf{x}; \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML})$ consistently estimates the minimum Kullback–Leibler divergence approximation of $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x})$ among all probability distributions of the form $g(y, \mathbf{x}; \mathbf{t})$. That is, assuming that there exists a unique $\tilde{\boldsymbol\theta} = \arg\min_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\mathrm{KL}\left[f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(\cdot|\mathbf{x})\,\|\,g(\cdot, \mathbf{x}; \mathbf{t})\right]$, then $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} \xrightarrow{p} \tilde{\boldsymbol\theta}$. canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 7.2.8 (Placebo Testing), the $F$-test passage, as printed
canonical_claim.statement: However, depending on the substance of the study in question, it is sometimes possible to present statistical evidence that may strengthen the credibility of the research design. Suppose that we have an additional set of placebo (or negative control) variables $\mathbf{W}_i$ that we do not think we need to condition on and that are not causally affected by the treatment assignment. Then we can test the null hypothesis that $\mathbf{W}_i \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i|\mathbf{X}_i$. This is known as a placebo test.$^{14}$ One simple way to implement this is by performing an $F$-test. An $F$-test compares a regression of $D_i$ on $\mathbf{W}_i$ and $\mathbf{X}_i$ with a regression of $D_i$ on $\mathbf{X}_i$ alone, and asks: does adding $\mathbf{W}_i$ to the regression explain more of the remaining variation in $D_i$ than we would expect by chance? If so, then we can reject the null hypothesis that $\mathbf{W}_i$ is independent of $D_i$ conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$. [As a statement that can be tested] Under i.i.d. sampling and the null hypothesis $\mathbf{W}_i \perp\!\!\!\perp D_i|\mathbf{X}_i$, the test that rejects when the $F$-statistic for adding $\mathbf{W}_i$ to the OLS regression of $D_i$ on $\mathbf{X}_i$ exceeds the $(1 - \alpha)$ quantile of its reference distribution has rejection probability at most $\alpha$ in the limit as $n \to \infty$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: the potential outcomes model $Y_i = Y_i(1) \cdot D_i + Y_i(0) \cdot (1 - D_i)$ (Definition 7.1.1), the unit-level treatment effect $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$ (Definition 7.1.2), the ATE $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i]$ (Definition 7.1.3); i.i.d. sampling of units; random assignment (Definition 7.1.9); strong ignorability conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ (Definition 7.1.12); the treatment propensity function $p_D$ (Definition 7.1.15); conditional independence (footnote 6, p. 215); expected value, conditional expectation and the Law of Iterated Expectations (Chapter 2). [Footnote 14, p. 270] Placebo tests of this type should not be confused with balance tests after matching or inverse probability weighting. Balance tests are used to assess whether or not we have successfully implemented the matching or weighting algorithm. By Theorem 7.1.16 (Strong Ignorability and the Propensity Score), if we have the right propensity score specification, we know that the “balancing property” ensures that we will have statistical independence of $D_i$ and $\mathbf{X}_i$.
canonical_claim.note: The passage as printed, for the Moderate finding P001-C07-E007. The book does not state the test's reference distribution or its size; the last paragraph gives the validity claim that 'we can reject the null hypothesis' presupposes, which the counterexample refutes. Footnote 14 omits 'conditional on the propensity score' in its last clause (clarity note P001-C07-N007).

canonical_claim.statement: Theorem 3.2.8. Weak Law of Large Numbers (WLLN). Let $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ be i.i.d. random variables with finite variance $\mathrm{V}[X] > 0$, and let $\overline{X}_{(n)} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i$. Then $\overline{X}_{(n)} \xrightarrow{p} \mathrm{E}[X]$. [Footnote 10: Note that if $\mathrm{V}[X] = 0$, the result follows trivially.]
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: i.i.d. random variables and the convention that the unsubscripted $X$ denotes the common distribution (Definition 3.1.1 and p. 92); sample statistic $T_{(n)}$ (Definition 3.2.1); sample mean $\overline{X}$ (Definition 3.2.2); convergence in probability (Definition 3.2.6); convergence in distribution (Definition 3.2.22); asymptotic normality (Definition 3.2.28); empirical CDF $\hat F$ (Definition 3.3.1); statistical functional and plug-in estimator (Definitions 3.3.2, 3.3.3); and the definitions of Chapters 1 and 2 (expected value, variance, covariance, correlation).
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: [Proof, p. 100] By non-negativity of probability and Theorem 3.2.5, $\forall \epsilon > 0$ and every $n$: $0 \le \Pr\left[|\overline{X}_{(n)} - \mathrm{E}[X]| \ge \epsilon\right] \le \frac{\mathrm{V}[X]}{\epsilon^2 n}$; and $\lim_{n \to \infty}\frac{\mathrm{V}[X]}{\epsilon^2 n} = 0$, so by the Squeeze Theorem for Sequences (footnote 11) $\lim_{n \to \infty}\Pr\left[|\overline{X}_{(n)} - \mathrm{E}[X]| \ge \epsilon\right] = 0$. The finite lemmas are Theorems 3.2.3, 3.2.4 and 3.2.5 (the exact headline target for this claim).
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P001-ch03-H2 (consistency of the sample mean); it held up. The statement is about an infinite i.i.d. sequence $X_1, X_2, ...$ with finite variance. The proof of Theorem 3.2.19 cites this theorem for the squares $X_i^2$, for which its finite-variance hypothesis is not implied (finding P001-C03-E006, separate targets).

canonical_claim.location: p. 109 (PDF p. 127). Definition 3.2.23: p. 109. Definition 3.2.22: p. 108 (PDF p. 126)
canonical_claim.statement: Theorem 3.2.24. Central Limit Theorem. Let $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ be i.i.d. random variables with (finite) $\mathrm{E}[X] = \mu$ and finite $\mathrm{V}[X] = \sigma^2 > 0$, and let $Z$ be the standardized sample mean. Then $Z \xrightarrow{d} N(0, 1)$, or equivalently, $\sqrt{n}(\overline{X} - \mu) \xrightarrow{d} N(0, \sigma^2)$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: i.i.d. random variables and the convention that the unsubscripted $X$ denotes the common distribution (Definition 3.1.1 and p. 92); sample statistic $T_{(n)}$ (Definition 3.2.1); sample mean $\overline{X}$ (Definition 3.2.2); convergence in probability (Definition 3.2.6); convergence in distribution (Definition 3.2.22); asymptotic normality (Definition 3.2.28); empirical CDF $\hat F$ (Definition 3.3.1); statistical functional and plug-in estimator (Definitions 3.3.2, 3.3.3); and the definitions of Chapters 1 and 2 (expected value, variance, covariance, correlation). [Definition 3.2.23, p. 109] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$ with finite $\mathrm{E}[X] = \mu$ and finite $\mathrm{V}[X] = \sigma^2 > 0$, the standardized sample mean is $Z = \frac{(\overline{X} - \mathrm{E}[\overline{X}])}{\sigma[\overline{X}]} = \frac{\sqrt{n}(\overline{X} - \mu)}{\sigma}$. [Definition 3.2.22, p. 108] Let $(T_{(1)}, T_{(2)}, T_{(3)}, ...)$ be a sequence of random variables with CDFs $(F_{(1)}, F_{(2)}, F_{(3)}, ...)$, and let $T$ be a random variable with CDF $F$. Then $T_{(n)}$ converges in distribution to $T$ if, $\forall t \in \mathbb{R}$ at which $F$ is continuous, $\lim_{n \to \infty} F_{(n)}(t) = F(t)$. We write $T_{(n)} \xrightarrow{d} T$. [Definition 2.1.19, p. 55 (PDF p. 73)] $N(\mu, \sigma^2)$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: For each fixed $n$: $\mathrm{E}[\overline{X}] = \mu$ (Theorem 3.2.3), $\mathrm{V}[\overline{X}] = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}$ (Theorem 3.2.4), hence $\sigma[\overline{X}] = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$, the two expressions for $Z$ in Definition 3.2.23 agree, and $\mathrm{E}[Z] = 0$, $\mathrm{V}[Z] = \sigma[Z] = 1$ (stated on p. 109). The book omits the proof of the theorem (footnote 19).
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P001-ch03-H4 (the standardized sample mean converges in distribution to $N(0, 1)$); it held up. The book states the theorem without proof. The 'equivalently' rests on Slutsky's Theorem (Theorem 3.2.25, p. 110).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Theorem 3.3.8 (Consistency of the Kernel Density Estimator, Rectangular Kernel)
canonical_claim.location: p. 122 (PDF p. 140); proof sketch on p. 123 (PDF p. 141); the continuity condition is stated on p. 121 (PDF p. 139)
canonical_claim.statement: [p. 121] In order for kernel density estimates to be consistent, we will need the bandwidth $h$ to tend to zero as $n$ tends to infinity. Then, as long as the PDF really is continuous, kernel density estimation will be consistent. Theorem 3.3.8. Consistency of the Kernel Density Estimator (Rectangular Kernel). For i.i.d. continuous random variables $X_1, X_2, ..., X_n$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$, if $K(x) = \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{I}(-1 \le x \le 1)$ (that is, the kernel is rectangular), and if $h \to 0$ and $nh \to \infty$ as $n \to \infty$, then $\hat f_K(x) \xrightarrow{p} f(x)$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: i.i.d. random variables and the convention that the unsubscripted $X$ denotes the common distribution (Definition 3.1.1 and p. 92); sample statistic $T_{(n)}$ (Definition 3.2.1); sample mean $\overline{X}$ (Definition 3.2.2); convergence in probability (Definition 3.2.6); convergence in distribution (Definition 3.2.22); asymptotic normality (Definition 3.2.28); empirical CDF $\hat F$ (Definition 3.3.1); statistical functional and plug-in estimator (Definitions 3.3.2, 3.3.3); and the definitions of Chapters 1 and 2 (expected value, variance, covariance, correlation). [Definition 3.3.7, p. 121] $K_h(x) = \frac{1}{h}K(\frac{x}{h})$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$ and $h > 0$; $\hat f_K(x) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} K_h(x - X_i)$, $\forall x \in \mathbb{R}$; $f$ is the common PDF of the i.i.d. continuous random variables $X_1, ..., X_n$. [p. 122] the definition of the PDF: $f(x) = \frac{dF(x)}{dx} = \lim_{h \to 0^+}\frac{F(x + h) - F(x - h)}{2h}$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: [From the proof sketch, p. 123; exact for each $n$ and $h > 0$] $\hat f_K(x) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\mathrm{I}(x - h \le X_i \le x + h)}{2h}$, an average of i.i.d. terms; hence $\mathrm{E}[\hat f_K(x)] = \frac{F(x + h) - F(x - h)}{2h}$ and $\mathrm{V}[\hat f_K(x)] = \frac{p_h(1 - p_h)}{4nh^2}$ with $p_h = F(x + h) - F(x - h)$ (Theorems 3.2.3 and 3.2.4 applied to the indicators), so that $\mathrm{V}[\hat f_K(x)] \le \frac{1}{2nh}\cdot\frac{F(x + h) - F(x - h)}{2h}$; and $\lim_{h \to 0}\frac{F(x + h) - F(x - h)}{2h} = f(x)$ at every $x$ where $F$ is differentiable with derivative $f(x)$. The variance bound is not printed; the book says only that 'the condition that $nh \to \infty$ is sufficient to guarantee that this limit carries through in estimation'.
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P001-ch03-H6; it held up, with a clarity note (P001-C03-A001): the box says 'for all $x$' without the continuity of the density that the preceding sentence requires; read with that sentence the theorem is correct, and it fails only at jumps of the density (for example the endpoints of $U(0, 1)$). A faithful statement therefore takes $x$ to be a point at which $f$ is continuous (or $F$ is differentiable with $F'(x) = f(x)$). The bandwidth is a deterministic sequence $h = h_n$.

canonical_claim.location: p. 125 (PDF p. 143); proof on pp. 125–126 (PDF pp. 143–144). Definition 3.4.1: p. 124 (PDF p. 142)
canonical_claim.statement: [p. 125] By asymptotically valid, we mean that $\lim_{n \to \infty}\Pr[\theta \in CI_{1-\alpha}(\theta)] \ge 1 - \alpha$. Theorem 3.4.2. Normal Approximation–Based Confidence Interval. Let $\hat\theta$ be an asymptotically normal estimator of $\theta$, $\hat{\mathrm{V}}[\hat\theta]$ be an consistent estimator of the sampling variance, and $\alpha \in (0, 1)$. Then an asymptotically valid normal approximation–based confidence interval for $\theta$ with coverage $(1 - \alpha)$ is given by $CI_{1-\alpha}(\theta) = \left(\hat\theta - z_{1-\frac{\alpha}{2}}\sqrt{\hat{\mathrm{V}}[\hat\theta]},\ \hat\theta + z_{1-\frac{\alpha}{2}}\sqrt{\hat{\mathrm{V}}[\hat\theta]}\right)$, where $z_c$ denotes the $c^{\mathrm{th}}$ quantile of the standard normal distribution; that is, $\Phi(z_c) = c$, $\forall c \in (0, 1)$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: i.i.d. random variables and the convention that the unsubscripted $X$ denotes the common distribution (Definition 3.1.1 and p. 92); sample statistic $T_{(n)}$ (Definition 3.2.1); sample mean $\overline{X}$ (Definition 3.2.2); convergence in probability (Definition 3.2.6); convergence in distribution (Definition 3.2.22); asymptotic normality (Definition 3.2.28); empirical CDF $\hat F$ (Definition 3.3.1); statistical functional and plug-in estimator (Definitions 3.3.2, 3.3.3); and the definitions of Chapters 1 and 2 (expected value, variance, covariance, correlation). [Definition 3.4.1, p. 124] A valid confidence interval for $\theta$ with coverage $(1 - \alpha)$ is a random interval $CI_{(1-\alpha)}(\theta)$, such that $\Pr[\theta \in CI_{(1-\alpha)}(\theta)] \ge 1 - \alpha$. [Footnote 34] A random interval is simply an interval formed by a pair of random variables. Suppose we have two random variables $C_1, C_2$, with $\Pr[C_1 < C_2] = 1$. Then $C = (C_1, C_2)$ is an (open) random interval. [Definition 3.2.28, p. 112 (PDF p. 130)] $\hat\theta$ is asymptotically normal if $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta - \theta) \xrightarrow{d} N(0, \phi^2)$, for some finite $\phi > 0$. [Definition 3.2.32, pp. 113–114, as corrected under P001-C03-N007] $\hat{\mathrm{V}}[\hat\theta]$ is consistent if $n\hat{\mathrm{V}}[\hat\theta] \xrightarrow{p} \mathrm{V}[T]$, where $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta - \theta) \xrightarrow{d} T$; here $\mathrm{V}[T] = \phi^2$. [Example 1.2.19, pp. 28–29 (PDF pp. 46–47)] $\Phi$ is the CDF of the standard normal distribution.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: [From the proof, pp. 125–126] For each $n$, with $Z = \frac{\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta - \theta)}{\phi}$ and $Z' = \frac{\hat\theta - \theta}{\sqrt{\hat{\mathrm{V}}[\hat\theta]}}$: $Z' = Z\frac{\phi}{\sqrt{n\hat{\mathrm{V}}[\hat\theta]}}$ exactly (where $\hat{\mathrm{V}}[\hat\theta] > 0$); and $\theta \in CI_{1-\alpha}(\theta)$ if and only if $-z_{1-\frac{\alpha}{2}} < Z' < z_{1-\frac{\alpha}{2}}$. The limit step uses $\sqrt{n\hat{\mathrm{V}}[\hat\theta]} \xrightarrow{p} \phi$ (CMT), Slutsky's Theorem ($Z' \xrightarrow{d} N(0, 1)$), and $\Phi(z_{1-\frac{\alpha}{2}}) - \Phi(-z_{1-\frac{\alpha}{2}}) = 1 - \alpha$.
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P001-ch03-H7; it held up. The limit of the coverage probability equals $1 - \alpha$ exactly (a candidate about open and closed endpoints in the proof, P001-C03-N013, was not confirmed: the normal limit is continuous). 'an consistent' is as printed (a typographical slip recorded under P001-C03-N010).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Theorem 5.2.6 (Consistency of the Maximum Likelihood Estimator) and the lemma in its proof sketch
canonical_claim.location: Theorem 5.2.6: p. 193 (PDF p. 211). Proof sketch: pp. 193–194 (PDF pp. 211–212)
canonical_claim.statement: Theorem 5.2.6. Consistency of the Maximum Likelihood Estimator. Let $Y$ be a random variable and $\mathbf{X}$ be a random vector. Let $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), (Y_2, \mathbf{X}_2), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$ be i.i.d. observations of $(Y, \mathbf{X})$. If the parametric model $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x}) = g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta)$ is true and some requisite regularity conditions (such as having a continuous likelihood function, a compact parameter space, and a unique maximum) are satisfied, then $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} \xrightarrow{p} \boldsymbol\theta$. [Proof sketch, pp. 193–194] Let $L_n(\mathbf{t}) = \frac{1}{n}\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X})$. By definition (and the assumption of a unique maximum), $\mathbf{t} = \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML}$ uniquely maximizes $L_n(\mathbf{t})$. Now, note that $\frac{1}{n}\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log g(Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i; \mathbf{t})$. This is a sample mean, so by the WLLN, $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log g(Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i; \mathbf{t}) \xrightarrow{p} \mathrm{E}[\log g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \mathbf{t})]$. Let $L(\mathbf{t}) = \mathrm{E}[\log g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \mathbf{t})] = \mathrm{E}[\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y, \mathbf{X})]$, so that $L_n(\mathbf{t}) \xrightarrow{p} L(\mathbf{t})$. We now require the following lemma: $\forall\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta$, $L(\mathbf{t}) \le L(\boldsymbol\theta)$, with $L(\mathbf{t}) = L(\boldsymbol\theta) \iff \Pr[g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \mathbf{t}) = g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \boldsymbol\theta)] = 1$. We omit the proof of this lemma. So we have shown that $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML}$ uniquely maximizes $L_n(\mathbf{t})$, $L_n(\mathbf{t}) \xrightarrow{p} L(\mathbf{t})$, and $\boldsymbol\theta$ uniquely maximizes $L(\mathbf{t})$. Given suitable regularity conditions, the ML estimate $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} \xrightarrow{p} \boldsymbol\theta$, so $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML}$ is consistent.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: parametric model and its truth (Definition 5.1.1); likelihood function (Definition 5.2.1); maximum likelihood estimator (Definition 5.2.2); the CEF (Definitions 2.2.15, 2.3.4); convergence in probability (Definition 3.2.6); i.i.d. observations $(Y_1, \mathbf{X}_1), ..., (Y_n, \mathbf{X}_n)$ of $(Y, \mathbf{X})$. [Definition 5.1.1, pp. 178–179 (PDF pp. 196–197)] Parametric Model. For a random variable $Y$ and random vector $\mathbf{X}$ of length $K$, a parametric model is a set of functions $g : \mathbb{R}^{K+1} \to \mathbb{R}$ indexed by a real-valued parameter vector $\boldsymbol\theta$ of length $\tau$: $\{g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta) : \boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta\}$, where $\boldsymbol\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}^\tau$. The set $\boldsymbol\Theta$ is called the parameter space. The model is said to be true if $\exists\boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta$ such that $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x}) = g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta)$. [Definition 5.2.1, p. 186 (PDF p. 204)] Likelihood Function. Let $Y$ be a random variable and $\mathbf{X}$ be a random vector, and assume the parametric model $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x}) = g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta)$. Then the likelihood function is $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y, \mathbf{X}) = g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \mathbf{t})$. For i.i.d. observations, $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$. [Definition 5.2.2, pp. 186–187 (PDF pp. 204–205)] Maximum Likelihood Estimator. For the parametric model $f_{Y|\mathbf{X}}(y|\mathbf{x}) = g(y, \mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol\theta)$ with $\boldsymbol\theta \in \boldsymbol\Theta$, the maximum likelihood estimator of $\boldsymbol\theta$ is $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X}) = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$, or, equivalently, $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_{ML} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}[\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X})] = \arg\max_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|Y_i, \mathbf{X}_i)$, where $\log\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{Y}, \mathbb{X})$ is known as the log-likelihood.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: [The lemma, exact] If the model is true at $\boldsymbol\theta$ and the expectations are finite, then for every $\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta$, $L(\mathbf{t}) - L(\boldsymbol\theta) = \mathrm{E}\left[\log\frac{g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \mathbf{t})}{g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \boldsymbol\theta)}\right] \le \mathrm{E}\left[\frac{g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \mathbf{t})}{g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \boldsymbol\theta)} - 1\right] \le 0$, using $\log z \le z - 1$ and the fact that $g(\cdot, \mathbf{x}; \mathbf{t})$ sums or integrates to at most 1 over the support of the true conditional distribution; equality holds if and only if $g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \mathbf{t}) = g(Y, \mathbf{X}; \boldsymbol\theta)$ with probability one. [A sufficient set of 'requisite regularity conditions', as made explicit by the validators of P001-C05-E001 and P001-C05-N005] (1) $\sup_{\mathbf{t} \in \boldsymbol\Theta}|L_n(\mathbf{t}) - L(\mathbf{t})| \xrightarrow{p} 0$; (2) $\boldsymbol\Theta$ compact, $L$ continuous and uniquely maximized at $\boldsymbol\theta$; then for every $\epsilon > 0$, with $\delta = L(\boldsymbol\theta) - \max_{\|\mathbf{t} - \boldsymbol\theta\| \ge \epsilon} L(\mathbf{t}) > 0$, on the event $\sup|L_n - L| < \delta/3$ no maximizer of $L_n$ lies at distance $\ge \epsilon$ from $\boldsymbol\theta$.
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P001-ch05-H4 (if the model is true and regularity conditions hold, the ML estimator is consistent); it held up, and a candidate about its regularity conditions (P001-C05-A004) was not confirmed. The book's statement is informal by its own description ('a slightly informal statement'); a faithful formalization must name the regularity conditions, and the pointwise convergence $L_n(\mathbf{t}) \xrightarrow{p} L(\mathbf{t})$ of the sketch is not by itself sufficient (a uniform version is the standard requirement). The prose on p. 194 says 'likelihood' where log-likelihood is meant (clarity note P001-C05-E008).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Theorem 6.1.4 (Estimating Sharp Bounds for the Expected Value)
canonical_claim.statement: Theorem 6.1.4. Estimating Sharp Bounds for the Expected Value. Let $Y_i$ and $R_i$ be random variables with $\mathrm{Supp}[Y_i] \subseteq [a, b]$ and $\mathrm{Supp}[R_i] = \{0, 1\}$, and let $Y_i^* = Y_iR_i + (-99)(1 - R_i)$. Then, given $n$ i.i.d. observations of $(Y_i^*, R_i)$, the plug-in estimator $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(Y_i^*R_i + a(1 - R_i)\right)$ is unbiased and consistent for the lower bound for $\mathrm{E}[Y_i]$. Likewise, the plug-in estimator $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(Y_i^*R_i + b(1 - R_i)\right)$ is unbiased and consistent for the upper bound for $\mathrm{E}[Y_i]$. [The bounds, from Theorem 6.1.3] lower bound $\mathrm{E}[Y_i^*|R_i = 1]\Pr[R_i = 1] + a\Pr[R_i = 0]$; upper bound $\mathrm{E}[Y_i^*|R_i = 1]\Pr[R_i = 1] + b\Pr[R_i = 0]$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: the stable outcomes model $Y_i^* = Y_iR_i + (-99)(1 - R_i)$ with response indicator $R_i$ (Definition 6.1.1); i.i.d. sampling of units; MCAR (Definition 6.1.5); MAR conditional on $\mathbf{X}_i$ (Definition 6.1.8) and conditional independence (footnote 6, p. 215); the response propensity function $p_R$ (Definition 6.1.11); expected value, conditional expectation and the Law of Iterated Expectations (Chapter 2). [Definition 6.1.1, pp. 208–209 (PDF pp. 226–227)] Stable Outcomes Model. For an outcome variable $Y_i$, the stable outcomes model is $Y_i^* = -99$ if $R_i = 0$ and $Y_i$ if $R_i = 1$; that is, $Y_i^* = Y_iR_i + (-99)(1 - R_i)$, where $Y_i^*$ is the censored version of $Y_i$ and $R_i$ is an indicator for whether $Y_i$ is observed for unit $i$. [Theorem 3.2.3, p. 97 (PDF p. 115)] For i.i.d. random variables $X_1, ..., X_n$, $\mathrm{E}[\overline{X}] = \mathrm{E}[X]$. [Theorem 3.2.8, p. 100 (PDF p. 118)] the WLLN for i.i.d. random variables with finite variance.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: [Proof, p. 212; exact] Let $Y_i^L = Y_i^*R_i + a(1 - R_i)$. Then $\mathrm{E}[Y_i^L] = \mathrm{E}[Y_i^L|R_i = 1]\Pr[R_i = 1] + \mathrm{E}[Y_i^L|R_i = 0]\Pr[R_i = 0] = \mathrm{E}[Y_i^* \cdot 1 + a \cdot 0|R_i = 1]\Pr[R_i = 1] + \mathrm{E}[Y_i^* \cdot 0 + a \cdot 1|R_i = 0]\Pr[R_i = 0] = \mathrm{E}[Y_i^*|R_i = 1]\Pr[R_i = 1] + a\Pr[R_i = 0]$; so for each $n$, $\mathrm{E}[\overline{Y_i^L}] = \mathrm{E}[Y_i^L]$ equals the lower bound (Theorem 3.2.3). The same with $b$ for $Y_i^U = Y_i^*R_i + b(1 - R_i)$. $Y_i^L$ and $Y_i^U$ take values in $[a, b]$, so their variances are finite and Theorem 3.2.8 gives consistency (footnote 10, p. 100, covers zero variance).
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P001-ch06-H1 (the plug-in estimators of the two end points are unbiased and consistent); it held up. Unbiasedness is exact for each $n$; consistency is the limit. The proof of the companion Theorem 7.1.8 in Chapter 7 has two misprinted symbols (finding P001-C07-E001, separate target).
